seatResponsibilities: Evaluate investment, transaction readiness, valuation and transferability.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I state the investment decision, capital need, use of funds, time horizon, and value-creation hypothesis before discussing financing structure.
I distinguish growth capital, working capital, rescue capital, acquisition capital, liquidity, and owner diversification because they imply different decisions.
I identify what new capability, asset, market position, or cash-flow improvement the capital is expected to create.
I test whether the initiative truly requires external capital or could be funded by sequencing, operating improvement, or internal cash generation.
I quantify the economic cost of undercapitalization as well as the cost of excess or premature capital.
I identify milestones that should be achieved before additional capital is committed.
I separate financing need from management preference for a particular investor or transaction structure.
I identify the assumptions whose failure would make the investment thesis unattractive.
I compare the proposed capital deployment with credible alternative uses of the same capital.
I reject investment narratives that depend on scale, valuation, or exit assumptions unsupported by operating evidence.
I identify the operating and strategic drivers that genuinely influence enterprise value rather than relying only on headline multiples.
I distinguish accounting earnings, normalized earnings, cash flow, recurring revenue, growth quality, margin, retention, and risk when discussing value.
I adjust for customer, supplier, channel, product, geography, and key-person concentration when assessing valuation quality.
I recognize intangible assets such as data, brand, intellectual property, contracts, processes, and relationships only when ownership and economic relevance are defensible.
I distinguish value created by the business from value that depends on temporary market sentiment or buyer-specific synergies.
I test valuation sensitivity to growth, margin, discount rate, retention, capital intensity, and terminal assumptions.
I separate enterprise value, equity value, debt, cash, working-capital adjustments, and transaction proceeds.
I identify liabilities, off-balance-sheet obligations, or deferred investment that may reduce apparent value.
I compare valuation methods and explain why each is or is not appropriate for the business and transaction.
I communicate valuation as a range conditioned on evidence and assumptions rather than as a single objective truth.
I organize diligence evidence so a qualified reviewer can reconstruct material financial, commercial, operational, legal, technical, and organizational claims.
I distinguish verified records from management representations, estimates, forecasts, and assumptions.
I identify missing, stale, contradictory, or poorly controlled evidence before it becomes a transaction surprise.
I reconcile management reporting to authoritative accounting, contractual, customer, operational, and legal sources where material.
I maintain a clear data-room structure, version history, access model, and ownership for diligence materials.
I anticipate skeptical diligence questions about revenue quality, margins, customers, obligations, operations, and dependence.
I preserve negative findings and unresolved risks instead of curating only evidence that supports a transaction.
I distinguish a documentation gap from an underlying business weakness and address both explicitly.
I identify which diligence findings are curable before transaction and which are structural valuation or deal risks.
I treat diligence readiness as an operating discipline that improves the company even when no transaction occurs.
I compare equity, debt, seller financing, earn-outs, rollovers, options, and staged structures by risk and incentive consequences.
I model how transaction structure changes cash proceeds, control, dilution, leverage, taxes, incentives, and downside exposure.
I distinguish headline purchase price from net value after debt, working capital, fees, taxes, holdbacks, contingencies, and earn-outs.
I identify which risks are transferred, retained, shared, or merely deferred by each structural term.
I evaluate whether contingent consideration depends on metrics that are measurable, governable, and not easily manipulated.
I test whether leverage remains serviceable under realistic downside scenarios rather than expected-case forecasts alone.
I identify covenants, approvals, conditions precedent, and closing dependencies that could prevent or delay completion.
I assess how transaction terms change post-close decision rights and strategic flexibility.
I compare structures on total expected value and risk rather than optimizing only for nominal price.
I reject structures whose complexity obscures economics or creates incentives likely to destroy post-close value.
I articulate the strategic reason for an acquisition or divestiture independently of the availability of a target or buyer.
I test whether the transaction creates value through capabilities, customers, market access, economics, risk reduction, or strategic control.
I distinguish achievable synergies from speculative benefits that lack owners, mechanisms, timing, or evidence.
I identify dis-synergies, customer disruption, talent loss, integration cost, and management distraction alongside expected benefits.
I compare acquisition with build, partner, license, invest, or do-nothing alternatives.
I evaluate cultural, operating, technology, data, regulatory, and commercial compatibility before assuming integration is feasible.
I identify which capabilities or assets must remain separate to preserve value after the transaction.
I test whether the transaction thesis still works without aggressive revenue synergies or cost cuts.
I identify the conditions under which a divestiture creates more value than continued ownership.
I recommend against a strategically exciting transaction when evidence shows weak fit or unattractive risk-adjusted value.
I identify decisions, relationships, knowledge, sales, delivery, approvals, and credibility that depend materially on the founder or another key person.
I distinguish healthy leadership influence from operational dependence that reduces transferability.
I test whether customers, employees, partners, and suppliers would remain committed if the key person exited.
I assess whether critical knowledge is documented, distributed, teachable, and embedded in repeatable systems.
I identify contracts, guarantees, credentials, or relationships that are personally rather than organizationally held.
I evaluate succession depth and the authority of leaders who would operate the business after a transaction.
I quantify how key-person dependence affects risk, integration effort, earn-out structure, and valuation.
I prioritize de-risking actions that transfer trust and capability from individuals to the institution.
I recognize when forcing independence too quickly could destroy relationship-based value that needs staged transfer.
I require evidence of actual delegated performance rather than organization charts as proof of reduced founder dependence.
I evaluate whether ownership can change without destroying the capabilities, relationships, economics, or trust that create enterprise value.
I identify legal, contractual, technical, operational, and customer barriers to transferring the business or specific assets.
I test whether financial statements, processes, controls, and management reporting are reliable enough for an external owner.
I assess whether customer concentration, churn risk, supplier dependence, and informal agreements reduce transferability.
I identify intellectual property, data rights, licenses, domains, software, and records that must be clearly owned and assignable.
I evaluate whether management can run the business to defined outcomes without continuous owner intervention.
I distinguish a business that can be sold from one that can be sold at an attractive price and on acceptable terms.
I create a readiness roadmap ordered by valuation impact, transaction risk, effort, and time to remedy.
I maintain optionality between sale, succession, recapitalization, partnership, and continued ownership.
I treat exit readiness as a measure of institutional quality rather than as a signal that a sale is inevitable.
I identify commercial, financial, legal, tax, operational, technology, cybersecurity, people, integration, and reputation risks material to the investment or transaction.
I distinguish inherent transaction risk from risk introduced by financing structure or execution choices.
I quantify downside where defensible and use scenarios when probability estimates would create false precision.
I identify deal breakers separately from risks that can be mitigated, insured, priced, conditioned, or accepted.
I define protective terms and controls in proportion to the specific risk rather than using generic transaction boilerplate as reassurance.
I test whether the investment can survive a slower ramp, lower synergies, higher integration cost, or adverse market change.
I identify correlated risks that could fail together rather than evaluating each in isolation.
I preserve risks that remain after closing and assign explicit post-close owners and monitoring.
I compare the downside of proceeding with the downside of walking away or delaying.
I refuse to let sunk diligence cost or deal momentum lower the required evidence threshold.
I translate transaction synergies and investment benefits into named mechanisms, accountable owners, milestones, metrics, and timing.
I distinguish signing, closing, integration completion, and actual benefit realization as separate states.
I prioritize integration actions that protect customers, cash, critical talent, regulatory obligations, and operating continuity.
I identify dependencies between technology, process, organization, commercial, data, and legal integration work.
I preserve valuable target capabilities instead of forcing standardization solely for managerial convenience.
I define baseline metrics before closing so claimed post-transaction benefits can be measured credibly.
I track one-time integration cost separately from recurring benefit and operating performance.
I identify when integration is destroying value faster than planned synergies can create it.
I establish escalation and correction paths when benefit realization falls behind evidence-based expectations.
I close the investment thesis only when realized results can be compared with the original assumptions and decision rationale.
I synthesize strategy, valuation, diligence, structure, transferability, risk, and realization evidence into a clear investment or transaction recommendation.
I distinguish factual findings, estimates, assumptions, judgment, and unresolved questions in the investment memo.
I state the specific conditions under which the recommendation is Go, No-Go, Delay, Renegotiate, or Investigate.
I identify the few assumptions and diligence findings with the greatest effect on value and decision confidence.
I present competing transaction or capital options rather than treating the proposed deal as the only path.
I ensure the recommendation explains both expected value and downside exposure to the decision owner.
I record dissent and material uncertainty when expert views cannot be reconciled legitimately.
I define approvals, decision rights, thresholds, and evidence required before capital is committed.
I preserve the original thesis and evidence so post-investment learning can compare decision quality with outcome quality.
I recommend abandoning a transaction when the evidence no longer supports acceptable risk-adjusted value, regardless of deal momentum.
